newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia trade says China buys 700,000t Canadian wheat.
newsitem.headline: Asia trade says China buys 700,000t Canadian wheat.

text.p: Far Eastern grain traders said on Friday China recently bought 700,000 tonnes of Canadian wheat, bringing Beijing's total purchases from Canada for the current marketing year to 1.5 million tonnes.
"In the last 10 days, the Canadians have sold another 700,000 tonnes (of wheat to China)," one source said.
Loading would begin at the end of September, he said.
While the market talk could not be immediately confirmed, it was reported by traders in Singapore, Australia and Hong Kong.
China and Canada have a long-term agreement for the annual supply of significant quantities of wheat.
Canada sold 800,000 tonnes of wheat to China in early August. A Canadian trader said at the time the deal was just the beginning of this year's bilateral wheat programme.
A source in Hong Kong said C&F (cost and freight) values at Canadian ports were currently around US$210 a tonne.

As Beijing's central food trading arm, China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import Export Corp (Cofco), buys FOB (free on board), the price to China would probably be around $190 a tonne, he said.
"Cofco and the CWB (Canadian Wheat Board) have a special relationship, so the price would be more competitive," he said.

China is the world's biggest importer of wheat. In 1995 it bought 11.59 million tonnes. Imports are usually divided between the United States, Canada and Australia, with small amounts from Europe and South America.
This year, however, China is heading for a bumper wheat crop of 107 million tonnes and so, factoring in high 1995 imports, is not expected to need to import more than eight million tonnes.
Traders in Asia say they doubt China will take any wheat from the United States for the first half of the 1996/97 marketing year which began on August 1.
But they said China would have to buy U.S. wheat in the second half of the year because Canada and Australia would not be able to fulfill all its requirements.
China has cancelled orders for around 1.4 million tonnes of U.S. wheat due for delivery in the second half of 1996 because of this year's bumper domestic harvest.

Traders have said that as a result, Chinese grain authorities are having to dip into central reserves to provide flour millers with higher quality imported wheat to blend with the lower quality domestic product.

"The flour millers need imported wheat for their blends, and the provincial authorities are 'borrowing' from the state reserve to get the mills their foreign wheat," a veteran trader in Hong Kong said. These reserves would have to be topped up from somewhere, he said.

Australia could not be relied upon because weather problems kicked in every three or four years to reduce the wheat crop, he said. And Canada had many commitments and limits on both time and port facilties.
"China is going to have to buy from the U.S. again, there is no way they can not buy from the U.S," he said.
Chinese imports from Canada average around five million tonnes a year, and in 1995 were 5.2 million tonnes.
The Canadian trading source expressed confidence that Beijing would maintain that level of imports from Canada this year despite the fall in import requirements.
Imports from the United States in 1995 were 3.8 million tonnes.
